about.title: The Origin of Life
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. There are 35 short beats of roughly 50 seconds each, with question breaks. The class is split into evidence, then ideas, then the panspermia debate, so each piece gets its own time.

say.text: Welcome to class six. Last time we built the Earth and the Moon. Today's question is a big one: how did lifeless chemistry turn into living things?

show.text: The Origin of Life

say.text: A fair warning: nobody knows the full answer. So we'll meet several hypotheses. A hypothesis is an idea that can be tested but isn't proven yet.

show.text: Hypothesis = a testable idea, not yet proven

ask.right: An idea that can be tested but is not yet proven
wrong: A fact that nobody can ever question
A random guess with no reasoning behind it
A type of rock found in Australia
ask.why: Scientists use hypotheses as ideas to test. Some get supported and some get dropped. Scientists don't expect the origin of life to be fully understood soon, so we will meet several.

say.text: First, evidence that life really was here early. Meet the stromatolite: a layered rock built up over time by mats of microbes. Microbes are living things too small to see.

show.text: Stromatolite = layered rock built by microbes

ask.right: A layered rock built up by communities of microbes
wrong: A fossilized dinosaur footprint
A kind of volcano on the ocean floor
The skeleton of one large ancient animal
ask.why: Stromatolites are laminated structures formed by microbes trapping and binding sediment, layer on layer.

say.text: In Western Australia, stromatolites in a rock layer called the Dresser Formation are about 3.5 billion years old. That's more than 50 times older than the last T. rex.

show.text: 3.5 billion years

say.text: Picture flat layers, domes and cones sitting side by side in the rock, tilted a little by time. In 2019, scientists found microscopic microbe remains inside them.

show.text: A rocky outcrop in Western Australia with layered, dome-shaped and cone-shaped stromatolites, tilted slightly

ask.q: About how old are the Dresser Formation stromatolites?
wrong: About 3.5 million years
About 350 million years
About 4.5 billion years
ask.why: They are about 3.5 billion years old. About 4.5 billion years is roughly the age of the Earth itself, so these traces of life are about a billion years younger than the planet.

say.text: Here's a detail to remember. The oldest site is thought to be an ancient volcanic hot spring. Nearby hot-spring deposits pushed back the earliest known life on land by 580 million years.

show.text: Hot spring

say.text: Now a different kind of clue: chemistry. Carbon comes in a lighter kind, carbon-12, and a heavier kind, carbon-13. Living things' enzymes tend to prefer the lighter one.

show.text: Carbon-12 (light) vs carbon-13 (heavy)

ask.q: Why can extra carbon-12 in a rock hint at life?
ask.right: Living things tend to prefer carbon-12, so carbon they process ends up richer in it
wrong: Carbon-12 glows when life is nearby
Carbon-12 only forms inside volcanoes
Extra carbon-12 means the rock is very young
ask.why: The enzymes that fix carbon prefer the lighter carbon-12. A high carbon-12 share is therefore a possible signature of life, though not proof on its own.

say.text: In Australia's Jack Hills, a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon crystal holds two specks of graphite. Their carbon-12 is about 2 percent higher than Earth's average. Zircons are tough, so they can survive for billions of years.

show.text: A tiny zircon crystal under a microscope, with two dark flecks of graphite inside

say.text: But this clue is disputed. Many researchers hesitate to accept chemical clues alone. A critic notes a crack could have healed without trace and let carbon in later. The team saw no sign of a crack.

show.text: Possible sign of life, still debated

ask.right: No. It is a possible sign of life that experts still debate
wrong: Yes. It is confirmed by stromatolite fossils
Yes. Everyone agrees it came from a living cell
No. Everyone agrees it is just ordinary rock
ask.why: Some researchers think it is biological carbon. Others say chemical clues alone are not enough. It is a hint, not a settled fact.

say.text: Science also checks itself. In 2016, a team reported 3.7-billion-year-old stromatolites in Greenland. In 2018, another team argued those shapes were made by rock being squeezed and deformed, not by life.

show.text: 2016: Greenland shapes = microbe-built stromatolites | 2018: Greenland shapes = deformed rock, not life

ask.q: What did the 2018 re-examination of the Greenland shapes conclude?
ask.right: The shapes were probably made by rock deformation, not by life
wrong: The shapes were confirmed as the oldest fossils
The shapes were proved to be man-made
The shapes were shown to be 4.5 billion years old
ask.why: The 2018 team measured the 3D shape and chemistry and judged the shapes to be tectonic features. The 3.7-billion-year claim is therefore contested.

say.text: One more idea about timing. LUCA stands for Last Universal Common Ancestor: the ancient cell that every living thing today descends from. It's worked out by comparing genes, not by finding a fossil.

show.text: LUCA = Last Universal Common Ancestor

say.text: A 2024 study estimated LUCA lived about 4.2 billion years ago, as a complex microbe that did not need oxygen. But LUCA was not the first life. Earlier, simpler life may have come before it.

show.text: About 4.2 billion years ago (estimate)

ask.q: Was LUCA the very first living thing?
ask.right: No. It is the shared ancestor of all life today, and earlier life may have come first
wrong: Yes. It was the first cell ever to exist
Yes. It was the first animal
No. It was a dinosaur that lived later
ask.why: LUCA marks the ancestor we all share, not the beginning of life. The 4.2 billion year date is also debated, and some experts doubt that LUCA could have survived such a violent early Earth.

say.text: Let's put these claims side by side. The oldest well-supported evidence is the 3.5-billion-year stromatolites. The older claims are possible, but debated. One expert says no single site is 100 percent proof.

show.text: How far back do the claims go? (billions of years ago)

say.text: So life was here early, within about a billion years of Earth forming, and perhaps much sooner if older, debated claims hold. That makes our next question sharper: how does chemistry become life?

show.text: Part 2: How Could It Start?

say.text: Charles Darwin had a private guess. In a 1871 letter to a friend, he imagined life's chemistry forming in a small pond, and he called it a very big 'if'.

show.text: "...some warm little pond, with all sorts of ammonia and phosphoric salts, light, heat, electricity..." (Darwin)

say.text: In 1952, a young chemist named Stanley Miller, working with Harold Urey, sealed water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen in glass flasks. Sparks stood in for lightning. They ran it for a week.

show.text: A sealed glass apparatus: a flask of warm water, a chamber with electric sparks, and tubes looping between them

say.text: The water turned brown. It contained amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. Vials from the original experiment, re-tested after Miller died in 2007, held more than 20 kinds.

show.text: Amino acids = building blocks of proteins

ask.q: What did the Miller–Urey experiment show?
ask.right: Simple chemicals plus energy can make amino acids, the building blocks of proteins
wrong: It created a living cell in a flask
It proved life began in lightning storms
It made a complete strand of DNA
ask.why: It was a proof of concept: building blocks can form from simple ingredients. It did not make life, and it did not prove where life began.

say.text: There's a catch. Later work suggested the early air held more carbon dioxide and nitrogen than Miller used. So his flask shows what's possible, not exactly what happened.

show.text: Possible is not the same as proven

say.text: Now back to that hot spring. Some scientists look to land. Pools and hot springs are one candidate for where life began. One 2026 critic of the ocean-vent idea favors lakes.

show.text: Warm pools and hot springs

say.text: The other big candidate lies on the deep seafloor. Hydrothermal vents are cracks where hot, mineral-rich water comes out. The 'Lost City' field was found in the year 2000. Its chimneys are cooler, about 50 to 90 degrees Celsius.

show.text: A dark seafloor with pale, rocky chimneys releasing shimmering warm fluid

say.text: The 'alkaline vent' idea says the vent fluid and the seawater differ in acidity, like a tiny natural battery. Tiny pores in the chimney walls could have acted as the first little cells.

show.text: Alkaline vent hypothesis: a natural battery

say.text: A 2026 paper challenges that. It says the fluid only becomes strongly alkaline after it cools, so the strong 'battery' may not have existed. It adds that sulfide may have been scarce. Defenders are still refining the idea.

show.text: Vent idea: under challenge, not dead

ask.q: Why do some scientists doubt the alkaline vent idea?
ask.right: The strong acidity difference may only appear after the fluid cools, so the 'battery' may not have worked at real vent temperatures
wrong: Nobody has ever found a hydrothermal vent
Vents are too cold to have any chemistry
Miller–Urey proved life began in a pond instead
ask.why: The 2026 paper argues the strong gradient is measured after cooling, not at hydrothermal temperatures. That is a challenge to the idea, not a final answer.

say.text: So we have two main settings. Neither is proven. The honest summary: we don't yet know where life began.

show.text: Warm pools and hot springs: land-based, a hot spring fits the oldest known site | Seafloor vents: a battery-like energy source, now under challenge

say.text: Now a different puzzle: copying. In a cell, genes store instructions, and proteins called enzymes do the work.

show.text: Part 3: Copying and the RNA World

say.text: Here's the trap. Proteins are needed to copy and read the instructions, and the instructions are needed to make the proteins. Each needs the other. Which came first?

show.text: Chicken-and-egg problem

ask.q: What is the chicken-and-egg problem in the origin of life?
ask.right: Instructions and proteins each seem to need the other to exist
wrong: Eggs and chickens evolved at the same time
Water and rock cannot mix
Cells need sunlight to divide
ask.why: Modern cells need proteins to use genetic instructions, and instructions to make proteins. The 'RNA world' idea is one way out of this loop.

say.text: RNA is a cousin of DNA. It can store information, and it can also speed up reactions like an enzyme. RNA that does this is called a ribozyme. The 'RNA world' idea says RNA did both jobs first.

show.text: RNA world: RNA stores information AND speeds up reactions

ask.q: What makes RNA special in this idea?
ask.right: It can both store information and speed up reactions
wrong: It is the only molecule that dissolves in water
It is made of protein
It is always found inside asteroids
ask.why: Because RNA can do both jobs, it could break the loop: one molecule first, then DNA and proteins later.

say.text: There is real evidence. Catalytic RNAs were found in 1982 and 1983. And the ribosome, the machine that builds proteins in every cell, uses RNA at its core. The idea itself dates to the 1960s.

show.text: 1960s: idea proposed by Crick, Woese and Orgel | 1982–83: RNA that speeds up reactions found | Today: ribosome built around RNA

say.text: But the chemistry is hard. Making RNA's parts on the early Earth is difficult. The sugar ribose is not robust. RNA chains also fall apart in many conditions.

show.text: Unsolved: making RNA on the early Earth

say.text: There has been progress. John Sutherland's group in Cambridge showed that simple starting chemicals, like hydrogen cyanide, plus ultraviolet light can make precursors of sugars, amino acids and nucleotides.

show.text: Progress: Sutherland's cyanosulfidic chemistry

ask.q: Which statement fairly describes the RNA world idea today?
ask.right: It is a leading idea with real supporting evidence, but its chemistry still has unsolved problems
wrong: It has been fully proven in the lab
It was disproven the moment ribozymes were found
It says life began on asteroids
ask.why: Evidence like ribozymes and the ribosome supports it. Hard chemistry steps remain, and some scientists favor other ideas instead.

say.text: One more idea: the ingredients, or life itself, came from space. This is panspermia, from the Greek for 'seeds everywhere'. Its modern form was pushed by Svante Arrhenius in 1908.

show.text: Part 4: Did Life Come From Space?

say.text: Here's the key point. Panspermia doesn't explain how life began. It moves the question somewhere else. A 'directed' version, which Crick and Orgel floated in 1973, even imagines it was sent on purpose.

show.text: Panspermia: how life spread, not how it began

ask.q: What question does panspermia mainly address?
ask.right: How life or its ingredients got to Earth, not how life first began
wrong: How old the Earth is
Why stromatolites have layers
How the Moon formed
ask.why: Critics point out that panspermia relocates the origin question to another place. It does not answer it.

say.text: New evidence comes from asteroid samples brought back to Earth. Japan's Ryugu and NASA's Bennu contain amino acids and nucleobases. Nucleobases are the chemical 'letters' of DNA and RNA. There are five.

show.text: Five nucleobases found in both Ryugu and Bennu

say.text: Bennu also holds sugars, including ribose. Together with the nucleobases and phosphate, that means every component of RNA has now been found there. That is ingredients, not life.

show.text: Space delivers ingredients

ask.q: What did the Ryugu and Bennu samples contain?
ask.right: Building blocks of life, like amino acids, nucleobases and sugars, but not proof that life itself arrived
wrong: Living bacteria alive and growing
A complete DNA genome
Fossil cells with tiny cell walls
ask.why: The asteroid samples show life's ingredients are common in space. That does not show life itself arrived. The samples were handled with strict contamination checks.

say.text: One twist. Many molecules come in two mirror-image forms, like left and right hands. Life on Earth uses the left-handed amino acids. Bennu's came in equal left and right amounts.

show.text: A left hand and a right hand side by side as mirror images

say.text: That result challenges one idea, that life's left-handed preference came from space. So the question of why life picked one hand is still open too.

show.text: Why left-handed? Still open

say.text: Let's gather it up. What we know, and what we don't.

show.text: We know: life existed about 3.5 billion years ago; building blocks form easily, in labs and in space; all life shares a common ancestor | We don't know: where it began; which came first, RNA or something else; exactly when

say.text: For context, here is what else was happening. The Earth was young, and no rock that old survives. Only tough crystal grains remain from the earliest times.

show.text: 4.54 billion years ago: Earth forms | 4.4: oldest known zircon grains | 4.2: LUCA estimate | 4.1: Jack Hills graphite (debated) | 3.5: Dresser stromatolites, on an oxygen-free planet

say.text: And the research has its own timeline. People have been testing these ideas for over a century, and it's still going.

show.text: 1871: Darwin's pond letter | 1952: Miller experiment | 1960s: RNA world idea | 2000: Lost City found | 2009: Sutherland's nucleotide route | 2020–2025: asteroid samples analysed | 2024: LUCA study | 2026: vent paper challenges the idea

say.text: So what's the fairest summary? Pick the one you'd stand behind.

show.text: What can we fairly say?

ask.q: Which statement is the fairest summary of the origin of life?
ask.right: Life existed by about 3.5 billion years ago and building blocks are easy to find, but how and where it began is still open
wrong: Scientists have proved life began at seafloor vents
Scientists have proved life arrived from space
Miller made life in a flask, so the question is closed
ask.why: The evidence is good for when life existed and for how building blocks form. The leading ideas (pools, vents, RNA world, space delivery) are still being tested, so the main question stays open.

say.text: Next class, class seven: complex cells, oxygen and a changing planet. Once life exists, it begins to change the whole Earth. See you then.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The Earth forms. Life's story starts only a few hundred million years later, on this young planet.
The oldest known mineral grains (zircons) from Jack Hills form. No rock that old survives, and the oldest rock with a reliable age is 4.03 billion years old.
A 2024 gene-based study places LUCA, the ancestor of all living cells, around this time. The estimate is debated.
The Dresser stromatolites grow at what was probably a volcanic hot spring, on a planet with no free oxygen. They are more than 50 times older than the last T. rex.
Darwin writes his 'warm little pond' letter to a friend.
Stanley Miller, supervised by Harold Urey at the University of Chicago, makes amino acids in a flask.
The RNA world idea is proposed by Crick, Woese and Orgel in the 1960s. Walter Gilbert coins the name 'RNA World' in 1986.
The Lost City hydrothermal field is discovered near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Powner, Gerland and Sutherland publish a route to activated RNA building blocks under plausible early-Earth conditions.
Hayabusa2 delivers Ryugu material to Earth in December 2020. In January 2025, Bennu analyses report amino acids and all five nucleobases.
The 2024 LUCA study appears. A 2026 PNAS paper challenges the alkaline vent hypothesis.

other_side.claim: 3.7-billion-year-old stromatolites in Greenland are the earliest fossils of life.
other_side.other_view: A 2018 team argued the shapes are rock deformation, not biology. The 3.5-billion-year-old Australian stromatolites are the better-supported earliest fossils. A Smithsonian source quotes a researcher saying no site is 100 percent proof.

other_side.claim: The 4.1-billion-year-old graphite in a Jack Hills zircon is chemical evidence of life.
other_side.other_view: Many researchers are hesitant to accept chemical clues alone as proof. One concern is that a crack could have healed without a trace and let carbon in later. The discovering team saw no sign of a crack.

other_side.claim: LUCA, the common ancestor of all life, lived about 4.2 billion years ago.
other_side.other_view: The timing is debated, and some experts doubt such a complex organism could have survived so early. LUCA is also not the first life, only the ancestor we all share.

other_side.claim: Alkaline hydrothermal vents were probably where life began.
other_side.other_view: A 2026 PNAS paper argues the strong 'battery' effect and key chemistry would not have worked at real vent conditions. Its author favors lake settings. Defenders are still refining the idea, and a review earlier this year called vents a consistent hypothesis.

other_side.claim: An RNA world came before DNA and proteins.
other_side.other_view: The ribosome's RNA core and ribozymes support it. However, making RNA's parts and chains on the early Earth is very hard. One researcher proposes a 'protein world' instead and concludes that life never emerged by the RNA-world route.

other_side.claim: Asteroid samples show life's ingredients came from space (panspermia).
other_side.other_view: The samples show ingredients are common, but they don't show life arrived. Critics say panspermia only moves the origin question elsewhere. Panspermia supporters argue their case is far from dead. Ingredients may also have formed on Earth, since Miller-type experiments make them too.

other_side.claim: Life's left-handed amino acids came from a bias in material from space.
other_side.other_view: Bennu's amino acids came in equal left and right amounts, and Ryugu's did too. This challenges that idea.
